terminologyProfile.descriptionRule: Use measurable 3D graphics terms. Avoid vague words unless they are paired with concrete geometry/material/shader parameters.

objectClass.notes: Static monumental landmark building, exterior shell only. No interior geometry: a prop kit is only ever looked at from outside, so an interior costs draw calls, geometries and VRAM for something nobody sees. Nothing moves, so one root pivot and zero sockets is the correct contract. A village relic stupa: a stepped square terrace with redented corners and one arched niche per face, a bell dome on moulded rings, a square harmika, a sixteen-ring conical taper and a worn gilt needle finial. The registry notes name the readable feature exactly -- "stepped square base, rounded bell, ringed taper, needle spire" -- and every authoring decision here serves that profile rather than any surface.

reasoning: Silhouette is the whole subject and it is NOT simple: bell, ringed taper and needle are three different curvatures stacked on a stepped square, and the registry notes say that profile must survive at a distance where no surface detail is visible at all.
Component count is low on purpose. Every ring, moulding and step is a PROFILE POINT rather than a mesh, so richness costs triangles -- the axis with headroom -- instead of draw calls.
Occlusion risk is unusually low for this kit: the prop is four-fold symmetric, so the single plate showing two of the four faces effectively shows all of them.
Action readiness is minimal: static landmark geometry, cylinder collider, not breakable.

specDepthDecision.rationale: Profile-dominated rather than repetition-dominated, which is the opposite of the retail set. The one repeating element is the four arched niches, and they must be repetitionSystems: as four separate frames plus four separate back panels they would cost eight draw calls of the twelve available, for four copies of two geometries.

resolvedUnknowns: The four niches are authored IDENTICAL. The plate shows two of them and they match; whether the unseen two hold different images or are blocked up cannot be known from one view.

The plate's peeling, crazing, drip streaks and lichen are WEAR, and they are authored -- as two post-construction canvas tiles, not as the generator's five-canvas texture set. The tile repeats every 3 m, so the pattern on the unseen faces is the same pattern; where the real object's flaking actually sits cannot be known from one view.
The niches are authored as shallow blind recesses. The plate shows the interior of one and it is empty; whether the others hold Buddha images is not observable.
The terrace is a solid mass with no doorway. Village chedis are solid by construction, and the plate shows no opening -- but a plate cannot prove the absence of one on an unseen face.

Declared at 14 m against the plate's own proportions, which read closer to 12.5 m at this width. The registry notes call 14 m correct for a village chedi and the declaration wins; the extra height is carried by the spire rather than by stretching the bell.

definitionOfDone: Rendered model matches the reference silhouette, the 8.00 x 14.00 x 8.00 m proportions, the visible component hierarchy and the material response for a real-time browser prop.

Zero coincident co-facing surface pairs (check-coplanar clean).
Exactly one root pivot and zero sockets; cylinder collider; no destruction groups.
Every material declares textureless with named evidence.

pivotInventory.name: root
pivotInventory.justification: The ONLY mechanism this prop has. Static landmark geometry: nothing opens, turns or swings, so every part is fixed and gets no axis. A named pivot is a promise that a part turns on it.

actionReadiness.socketJustification: ZERO sockets, deliberately. Nothing attaches to this prop and nothing is emitted from it. A marker named for a place on the surface is a location, not a mechanism.

colliderInventory.note: Declared on the asset as CYLINDER rather than the building-part default box, and the asset notes give the reason: the bell and spire are round in plan, so a box proxy would leave a player colliding with empty air at the corners for eight of the prop's fourteen metres. One convex proxy over the whole envelope.

actionReadiness.destructionJustification: The asset declares destructionGroups as an empty list -- this prop is NOT breakable. No component carries actionProfile.destruction.fractureGroup. promote-model checks built against declared as an equality in BOTH directions, so an invented group fails the gate just as a missing one would.

silhouette.description: Read bottom to top: a stepped square pyramid of six redented slabs to 3.85 m; moulded rings at 2.70 m radius; a BELL whose body rises near-vertical from 2.36 m radius at 4.52 to 1.98 at 6.45 and rounds over a quarter-ellipse shoulder to a FLAT crown 1.30 m in radius at 7.72; a square harmika of 2.10 and 1.52 m from 7.55 to 9.05, its metre-tall lower block standing on the flat crown; a sixteen-ring conical taper from 0.66 m radius at 8.99 to 12.30 m; a gilt needle to 14.00 m. The silhouette events are the terrace steps, the foot rings, the bell's vertical flank turning into its dome, the harmika's square interruption of an otherwise round form, and the needle. The first build had the bell as a quarter-cosine ogive from the foot, pointed at 8.30 with the harmika floating 0.25 m above it; the profile is now the Meshy proxy's own radius-by-height, read at 56 slices.
silhouette.envelopeDerivation: x and z both span -4.00..+4.00 = 8.00, set by the bottom terrace slab: its redented plan has its widest point on the flat of each face at 4.00, and the corner redents cut INWARD from there, so the corners do not push the bounding box out past the faces. y spans 0.00 (terrace underside) to 14.00 (finial tip). Nothing else on the prop reaches any of those planes -- the niche frames stand proud to 3.30 and the bell to 2.70, both well inside 4.00 -- so the envelope is set by exactly two parts and can be read off them.
silhouette.meshyCrossCheck: Independent Meshy v7 reconstruction of the same plate normalises to w:h:d = 1 : 2.000 : 1.000 against the declared 1 : 1.750 : 1.000 -- depth EXACT, height 14% taller. That is the closest agreement of any prop in this batch and it agrees on the thing that matters: a chedi is a square-plan solid of revolution, and both readings say so. Area-weighted band comparison against the reference mesh gives mean |delta width| 0.019 and |delta depth| 0.019 of height with no band past 0.045. That is the REBUILT figure: the first build measured 0.030 with the spire bands 6-8 at +0.06, and the bell shoulder and harmika were then read off the proxy at 56 slices (scratch/_mon/profile.mjs) rather than off the three-quarter plate -- a near-vertical body, a domed shoulder, a 0.72 m neck and a 1.66 m harmika, and a spire starting at 0.68 m. The spire bands are now within 0.017. The declared 14 m wins and the extra height the proxy wants is not taken.

viewEvidence.note: NOT DIRECTLY OBSERVED, but confidence is 0.80 rather than the 0.20 this kit gives an unseen elevation: the prop is four-fold symmetric about its axis, so the rear faces are the same faces as the two the plate shows. What is genuinely unknown is only whether the real object's four niches differ from one another.

componentTree.name: Stepped terrace
componentTree.topologyRationale: Six stepped slabs in one material. Each is a single EXTRUSION of a closed redented plan rather than a wide box crossed by a deep one: crossed boxes put their top faces in the same plane facing the same way over the whole intersection, which z-fights, and one closed plan has no interior coincidence at all.

geometryDescriptor.topologyIntent: Six redented slabs from y=0.00 to y=3.85, widest at half-width 4.00 and stepping in to 2.86, with the fifth stepping back OUT as a cornice.
geometryDescriptor.zFightingNote: Consecutive slabs meet as OPPOSED faces -- one slab's top against the next slab's bottom -- which is how solids are meant to meet and does not fight. check-coplanar reports the prop clean at 0.001 m.
geometryDescriptor.mergeNote: Primitive is recorded as "extrusion" because that is what each slab is; the six are MERGED into one BufferGeometry and submitted as ONE draw call.

componentTree.name: Bell dome
componentTree.topologyRationale: A surface of revolution, so a lathe is the only honest primitive: a box decomposition of a bell is not a low-poly bell, it is a different object. The moulded rings at its foot and the drum neck at its crown are PROFILE POINTS on the same lathe, not separate meshes, which is what keeps the whole dome at one geometry and one draw call.

geometryDescriptor.topologyIntent: One lathe from y=3.70 to y=8.72: two mouldings at 2.70 m radius, a body from 2.36 at 4.52 to 1.98 at 6.45, a quarter-ellipse shoulder rounding over to a FLAT crown of 1.30 m radius at 7.72 (horizontal tangent), the crown running inward to a 0.75 m neck that rises to 7.90 inside the harmika block. Body and foot are the Meshy proxy's radius-by-height at 56 slices; the flat crown is the plate's, chosen over the proxy's domed cone, which kept climbing into the block.
geometryDescriptor.zFightingNote: The lathe's base is sunk to y=3.70, INSIDE the top terrace slab, and its top runs 0.15 m up INSIDE the harmika slab, which is seated down onto the dome's shoulder. LatheGeometry is open at both ends; an open rim sitting exactly on a surface is a seam the turntable gate can read through, and an open rim stopping 0.25 m SHORT of one -- the first build -- is a floating block.

The extractor palette is advisory only: these crops are flat material swatches, not isolated objects, so its foreground separation is weak by its own warnings. Albedo is the direct crop measurement.

evidence: Measured on viewEvidence region-finial (PBR confidence 0.860) at #94805F, the brightest gilt on the finial. The registry calls the finial gilded and it is, but the plate's gilding is WORN -- ochre with grey bare patches -- so this is the measurement rather than the word.

Metalness 0.30, far below physical: the harness supplies no environment map and a metal with nothing to reflect renders black, which on this prop would lose the only surface that is not grey. The albedo stays measured; the metalness is what the rig makes wrong.
textureless.note: Declared textureless so createSculptMaterial skips makeProceduralTextureSet entirely -- FIVE canvases per material written pixel by pixel, at a cost that is the SQUARE of the resolution. It is also a correctness fix: with a texture set the generator forces color to white and roughness to 1 and reads both from the generated maps, discarding this measured albedo.

repetitionSystems.name: Arched niche frames
repetitionSystems.rationale: One niche per face, four-fold symmetric. As four separate meshes they would cost four draw calls of twelve for four copies of one geometry.
repetitionSystems.zFightingNote: The frame is embedded 0.10 m into the terrace face and stands 0.30 m proud of it, so it OVERLAPS its opening rather than meeting the reveal edge -- the rule that stops a frame putting four coincident reveal faces in the model.

repetitionSystems.name: Niche back panels
repetitionSystems.rationale: The back of each niche, in its own darker material. A second system rather than a second colour on the first, because InstancedMesh takes one material.
repetitionSystems.zFightingNote: Stands 0.05 m PROUD of the terrace face rather than flush with it, and sits 0.23 m behind the frame's front plane. The depth is the feature: a niche is a concavity, and a flat dark rectangle painted on a wall is not one.

featureReviews.evidence: Six redented slabs from y=0.00 to 3.85 as one merged extrusion, with four arched aedicules standing 0.30 m proud and dark back panels 0.23 m behind their front plane. Unchanged in this round apart from the lichen tile.
featureReviews.notes: Two things here were learned by rebuilding. Each slab is an EXTRUSION of a closed redented plan rather than a wide box crossed by a deep one: crossed boxes put their top faces in the same plane facing the same way over the whole intersection and z-fight, while one closed plan has no interior coincidence at all. And the arch aperture was first written as an arc from PI to 0, which swept through the BOTTOM of the circle: the arch head was left filled solid with the arc's own seam z-fighting across it, giving a square window with a ghost arch drawn on it. The direction of a half-circle is not a detail on this prop; it is the feature. The niche storey was also re-proportioned to 1.70 m so a 1.45 m aedicule fits inside it -- sized the other way round, the arch head ran up through the cornice above and was swallowed.

featureReviews.evidence: Bell as one lathe: foot mouldings at 2.70, a body from r 2.36 at 4.52 to 1.98 at 6.45, a quarter-ellipse shoulder rounding over to a flat 1.30 m crown at 7.72, the harmika block standing on the flat with a 0.75 m neck running up inside it. Harmika 2.10 / 1.52 m square from 7.55 to 9.05, a metre-tall lower block seated down into the crown; spire from r 0.66 at 8.99 to 0.22 at 12.30, sixteen rings; closed gilt needle with a bud.
featureReviews.notes: The first build's bell was a quarter-cosine from the foot -- an OGIVE, full at the haunch and pointed at the top -- and it stopped at 8.30 with the harmika starting at 8.55, a 0.25 m air gap under a floating block. The proxy's radius-by-height says what a bell is: near-vertical flanks (2.36 at 4.1, 2.03 at 5.1, 1.90 at 6.4 in 14 m scale) that round over the top 1.3 m to a 0.72 neck, with a 1.66 m harmika on the neck. A quarter-ellipse shoulder was tried first and put band 5 at +0.07 -- a hemisphere, not a domed cone -- and the proxy's own normalised falloff (0.93, 0.85, 0.69, 0.44, 0.17) was fitted instead. The harmika, at 2.56 m in the first build, was read off the plate's diagonal and was 50% too wide; the spire base at 1.05 was what put bands 6-8 a twentieth of the height too fat. The lever remains the LATHE: the neck is two more profile points, not a mesh, and the prop is still 7 draw calls.

reviewHistory.summary: Structural pass: terrace as six merged extrusions of a redented plan, bell (with its neck) and spire as lathes, harmika as two boxes standing on the neck. The four niches are two repetition systems -- as eight separate meshes they would have cost eight draw calls of twelve for four copies of two geometries.

Returned after promotion: the bell was an ogive -- a quarter-cosine from the foot tapering to a 0.62 m point at 8.30 -- and the harmika started at 8.55, floating 0.25 m above it. Rebuilt the lathe from the Meshy proxy's radius-by-height (scratch/_mon/profile.mjs, 56 slices): near-vertical body, domed shoulder, drum neck run 0.12 m up inside the harmika slab; harmika resized to the proxy's 1.66 m; spire base slimmed from 1.05 to 0.66.

Returned again: the harmika on its 0.50 m visible neck still read as disconnected from the bell. Dropped it 0.45 m so the lower slab (8.15-8.55) is seated into the crown -- the dome shoulder at r 0.93 passes up inside the slab underside -- and the spire extended down to 8.99 to keep the 14 m height.

Returned a third time: the seated lower slab, at 0.40 m and proxy width, read as a thin wafer under the upper cube. Made it a 2.10 m block a metre tall (7.55-8.55), extended DOWN into the dome so its faces clear the shoulder at 7.98 and its corners at 7.50.

Returned a fourth time: with the block seated, the domed-cone shoulder no longer looked like the plate's bell. Reshaped the shoulder as a quarter-ellipse to a FLAT 1.30 m crown at 7.72, horizontal tangent at the top, the block standing on the flat. Band 5 moves away from the proxy (which reads a domed cone); the plate wins here on the user's call.

lodPlan.strategy: full component tree and material layers
merge static components and reduce local feature geometry

performanceBudget.optimizationPolicy: Real-time browser FPS prop on low-end integrated GPUs; a level builder places hundreds at once. All four ceilings come from thaikit resolveBudget() for the hero2x class and none was invented. The component split was costed against the DRAW-CALL ceiling in the blockout, before any geometry existed: parts that share a material are merged into one component rather than left to be merged later, because a pivot hung off a part cannot be merged afterwards.

drawCalls.note: Five components and two repetition systems: 7 of 12. The lever here is the LATHE, not the merge. Every moulding, ring and step is a profile point rather than a mesh, so the sixteen spire rings and the two bell mouldings cost zero draw calls between them.

materials.note: stucco covers the bell, the harmika AND the spire -- three components, one material, because they are the same whitewash and a colour difference would not have been a material difference even if there had been one. Four of eight materials, four in hand.

uniqueGeometries.note: One per component plus one per repetition system. A scaled box is NOT a shared geometry -- the generator bakes real dimensions in via geometry.scale(), so every differently-sized box is genuinely distinct. Each InstancedMesh reuses a single geometry across all its instances, which is the whole point.

triangles.note: Triangles are where this prop spends, and deliberately: 5,184 of 16,000, nearly half of it in the two lathes. That is the correct trade for a subject whose entire identity is its profile, and the headroom must not be read as room to split components -- draw calls are the scarce axis, at 7 of 12.

lightingFromPhoto.notes: The plate is a flat studio lightbox: surfaces at 90 degrees to each other measure within a few levels, which is only possible under near-shadowless illumination. That is WHY the measured crop means are usable as albedo with little correction.
High fill ratio inferred from the shadow-side wall retaining full value.

The seamless backdrop acts as a large uniform environment. The thaikit harness supplies NO environment map, which is why every metal on this prop carries a metalness well below its physical value -- a metal with nothing to reflect renders black.
NO rim light in the plate. Recorded so a missing rim in the render is not read as a defect.
Exposure 1.0 with ACES filmic tone mapping; no exposure compensation is applied to the measured albedos and none is warranted.

NO contact or ground shadow in the plate -- it is a cut-out against a seamless backdrop. Recorded so the absence is not read as a missing feature. IN USE this is a floor-placed building and the HOST scene owns its contact shadow: castShadow ships enabled on every mesh and the factory defines no ground plane of its own.

proceduralStrategy.strategy: Lathes and extrusions, not boxes. A bell, a ringed taper and a needle are surfaces of revolution and a box decomposition of one is not a low-poly version of it but a different object; the terrace is an extruded redented plan for the same reason -- crossed boxes would z-fight where they intersect. The only boxes on the prop are the harmika's two blocks and the niche back panels.
Two InstancedMesh systems carry 8 of the prop's 13 discrete parts, all four-fold symmetric about the axis.
All procedural variation is assigned by instance INDEX, never from a random source, so the model is byte-identical on every build.

Every material is declared textureless to the GENERATOR -- no five-canvas procedural set. Two Canvas 2D wear tiles (peel/crazing on the stucco, lichen/crazing on the stone) are drawn post-construction as a few hundred Path2D fills at 512 px and bound as map and bumpMap, the route the retail set uses for its fascias; no per-pixel JavaScript, and the measured albedo stays on the material as the multiplicand. The factory builds in ~80 ms with 2.7 MB of texture VRAM; under Node, with no DOM, the materials keep their flat measured colour.

risks.description: The plate's own proportions read closer to 12.5 m at this width, and Meshy reads it taller still at 16 m.
risks.mitigation: The declared 14 m is between the two and the registry notes call it correct for a village chedi. The extra height over the plate is carried by the spire rather than by stretching the bell, which is where a real chedi's height varies.

risks.description: The peel, crazing and lichen are a 3 m tile, so the same flake recurs around the bell about five times and on every terrace face.
risks.mitigation: The tile is seeded and seamless, the flakes are random walks with no strong axis, and at the distance a 14 m landmark is read the repeat is below notice. The alternative -- a projected plate crop -- would need the texture set that discards every measured albedo, and this prop is four-fold symmetric anyway.

risks.description: On the bell's foot mouldings the horizontal ledge faces share the cylindrical mapping's constant v, so the crack network runs radially across them.
risks.mitigation: The ledges are 2-20 cm deep on a 14 m prop; a per-face projection switch on an indexed lathe would smear the triangles that straddle it, which is worse.

risks.description: All four niches are authored the same; the plate shows two.
risks.mitigation: The prop is four-fold symmetric and the two visible niches match. Recorded as an assumption rather than closed silently.
